# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization is a family of mesh generation techniques that eliminate geometric primitives occluded by adjacent solid voxels, significantly reducing triangle count and rendering load in blocky voxel terrain [S1, S2, unofficial]. It differs from its siblings by operating on local geometric adjacency (neighbor checks) or view-dependent projection to determine face visibility, whereas methods like [Greedy face merging](8935-greedy-face-merging.md) focus on topology simplification and [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) relies on material transparency properties.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of rejecting faces that do not contribute to the visible surface of the voxel structure. The fundamental optimization is based on the observation that a voxel cube has 6 faces, but only those adjacent to empty space (or a different material class) are visible.

1.  **Neighbor Occupancy Check**: The primary determinant of face visibility is the state of the immediate neighbor voxel. If a neighbor at position $P + N$ (where $N$ is the face normal) is solid, the face at $P$ in direction $N$ is internal and culled [S1, S2, unofficial].
2.  **Boundary Definition**: A face is considered "exposed" if the neighbor is empty (air) or out of bounds [S2, unofficial].
3.  **Batching**: Individual voxel faces are aggregated into larger structures (chunks or meshes) to minimize draw calls, subject to GPU vertex limits (e.g., ~65,000 vertices in Unity) [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
A technique for dynamically updating a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed, using neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from its sibling [Greedy face merging](8935-greedy-face-merging.md) by maintaining per-block visibility flags rather than merging adjacent quads into larger primitives, and from [Blocky meshing](31-blocky-meshing.md) generally by focusing on incremental state updates rather than batch mesh generation.

### [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md)
A trait-based system that defines block geometry, transparency culling modes, and lighting properties per block type. It solves the problem of heterogeneous voxel rendering by allowing different block types to specify their own mesh generation rules and visibility constraints. Unlike standard boolean transparency flags, this system distinguishes between opaque, transparent-merged, and transparent-unmerged blocks, and supports complex geometries (ramps, fluids) via polymorphic builders. It builds on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by providing the per-block metadata required to execute those culling decisions.

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
A method for optimizing blocky mesh generation by representing the geometric coverage of a voxel face as a bit mask, allowing for the culling of partially occluded faces from partial shapes (such as stairs and slabs). Unlike basic neighbor checks that treat faces as binary solid/empty, this method solves the problem where a boolean solid flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. It sets itself apart from [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) by enabling fine-grained visibility decisions based on geometric overlap rather than simple adjacency, and from [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) by separating geometric coverage from material transparency properties.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
A dynamic mesh generation and buffer management technique for voxel terrain, designed to minimize GPU memory overhead and draw calls by packing vertex attributes into compact integer formats and reusing vertex slots. It solves the problem of sparse, high-latency buffer updates in incremental voxel editing by maintaining a contiguous vertex array with a free-list allocator, allowing faces to be added or removed without reallocating GPU memory. Unlike static meshing methods, it supports real-time block placement and removal by updating only the affected chunk and its immediate neighbors, leveraging the neighbor check principles of [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) to determine face visibility.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
This method optimizes voxel mesh generation by rejecting invisible faces in projection space and masking faces shared between neighboring voxels. It addresses the performance bottleneck of rendering internal geometry by combining view-dependent backface culling with topology-based internal face rejection. It differs from standard neighbor-check culling [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) by explicitly handling projection-space orientation to reject back-facing surfaces, while retaining the internal masking logic to skip shared faces.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
Block Visibility Culling determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering based on the camera's position and orientation, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the viewing direction changes minimally. It operates at the coarse block level by comparing camera coordinates and view vectors against block normals, distinguishing itself from sibling methods that operate at the fine-grained face level within a block.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
Extraction of Surface Points is a fast display method for the direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It solves the problem of high computational cost in volume rendering by avoiding the processing of occluded or internal voxels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by operating on a list of extracted 3D points (voxels) rather than generating polygonal meshes or chunks, and by using a multi-view orthographic projection strategy to determine visibility.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
Mask Projection Culling is a visibility-based mesh filtering technique that removes faces and vertices not consistently observed across multiple camera poses by projecting 3D points into camera space and comparing their depth against rendered depth maps or binary masks. It differs from neighbor-check culling (e.g., [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)) by relying on global view constraints rather than local voxel occupancy, and from simple back-face culling by utilizing multi-view consistency and depth testing to eliminate geometry occluded from all viewpoints.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method culls mesh geometry by projecting vertices into multiple camera views and comparing their depths against reference depth maps to identify and remove unseen or forecast geometry. It distinguishes itself from local neighborhood checks by using global multi-view consistency to filter artifacts from unbounded reconstructions, specifically targeting geometry that is not consistently visible across a set of camera poses.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization that prevents the rendering of block faces occluded by adjacent solid voxels, significantly reducing triangle count in homogeneous voxel terrain. It solves the problem of naively rendering all six faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, by skipping the addition of faces adjacent to existing neighboring voxels to the vertex buffer. Unlike [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) which operates on whole blocks or [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) which considers material properties, Face Culling relies strictly on local geometric adjacency.

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
Opacity-based Mesh Culling is a post-processing technique for converting volumetric or implicit radiance field representations into explicit polygonal meshes by discarding geometric primitives that contribute negligible visual information. It solves the problem of excessive mesh complexity and storage overhead inherent in raw neural rendering outputs. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial occupancy or face coverage masks, this method evaluates the optical depth (opacity) of individual triangles or mesh blocks to determine visibility, retaining only those elements that exceed a defined opacity threshold.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
From-region visibility preprocessing is a technique that precomputes which geometric primitives are visible from a specific region of the viewing space, allowing for aggressive culling of occluded geometry during rendering. It differs from sibling methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) or [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) by operating on large-scale scene geometry (often millions of triangles) rather than local voxel occupancy, and by focusing on global occlusion relationships rather than local surface continuity.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The process involves resetting the buried bitmask for the chunk, creating `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterating through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`) to determine if each is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and setting the corresponding flag in the bitmask [S2, unofficial]. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped [S2, unofficial]. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The first pass (opaque) generates faces for opaque blocks; if the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air) to generate opaque faces between air and transparent blocks [S3, unofficial]. The second pass (transparent) tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks, generating faces for all transparent blocks touching air but not adding faces between transparent and solid blocks [S3, unofficial]. Solid block types are filtered out during the transparent pass by checking if the block type is not transparent before constructing the AO value and adding the block type to the hashmap [S3, unofficial].

### Smart Leaf Rendering
A leaf block rendering strategy that preserves alpha cutouts on outer leaf surfaces while culling internal faces to reduce vertex count [S4, unofficial]. It is controlled by a global static enum `sLeafRenderMode`, which defaults to `ChunkRenderer::LeafRenderMode::Smart` [S4, unofficial].

### Hidden Face Extension
A proposed optimization where the 2D grid includes a 'don't care' state (2) to allow rectangles to extend into hidden areas, potentially reducing total rectangle count [S5, unofficial]. While this might reduce mesh size, it increases the load on the rasterizer [S5, unofficial].

## Background
The technique originated as a solution to the inefficiency of rendering full cube models for voxel terrain. Early implementations, such as those described in procedural terrain generation literature, noted that a brute-force approach instantiating full cube models resulted in rendering 12 triangles (6 sides) per cube, even when only 2 triangles (1 side) were visible [S1, unofficial]. The optimization involved reconstructing cubes from triangles and removing sides adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of internal polygons [S1, unofficial]. This approach was further optimized by combining individual cube meshes into single "chunk" meshes, though this introduced GPU vertex count limits (e.g., ~65,000 vertices in Unity) [S1, unofficial]. The concept of "Removing Interior Polygons" has been a standard optimization in voxel engines since the early days of Minecraft-like terrain generation [S1, unofficial].
